description: We’re building an offline astronaut health monitoring app for NASA Space Apps. It tracks sleep, heart rate, mood, and stress, compares them to each astronaut’s personal baseline, flags worrying trends early with green/yellow/red alerts, and guides astronauts on what to do next, since help from Earth is far away on Moon or Mars missions.
summary:
Vitals in Orbit (V.I.O) is a health monitoring web app that helps astronauts track their own wellbeing on long-duration, deep-space missions. It gathers key health indicators and shows them as trends over time, so the crew member can see gradual “drift” away from their personal baseline before it becomes a serious problem.

This addresses the challenge directly. On long missions, radiation, isolation, altered gravity, and a closed environment can cause immune changes, bone loss, cardiovascular events, and behavioral health issues. Astronauts often must notice these changes in themselves, with limited real-time support from Earth. V.I.O gives them a clear view of their own health status and makes early warning signs easy to spot and act on.

This matters because small changes caught early are far easier to manage than emergencies discovered late. Self-directed monitoring improves crew safety and autonomy, and it supports mission success as humans travel farther from Earth.
details:
What it does / how it works
V.I.O is a web app for astronauts on long-duration missions. Each crew member has a profile with a personalized baseline and mission context. A guided daily check-in captures vitals, sleep, mood, nutrition, exercise, symptoms, and radiation exposure. An alert engine compares every reading against two references: the astronaut’s own rolling baseline and absolute physiological safety limits. It also looks for multi-day patterns, such as declining sleep, rising stress, or falling mood, even when the latest value is still in range. Composite rules combine related signals (poor sleep + high stress + low mood, or elevated heart rate + elevated temperature + fatigue) to flag behavioral and infection risks earlier. Results appear as a readiness score, hazard map, alert timeline, and mission routine reminders, with plain-language guidance on what to do. A printable ground-link summary can be shared with a flight surgeon.

Benefits

  • Catches gradual drift early, before symptoms escalate
  • Personal baselines make “normal” specific to each astronaut
  • Plain-language guidance helps astronauts act without a clinician on hand
  • Covers physical and behavioral health in one place
  • Works offline and keeps data private (local-first, no external calls)

Intended impact
To give astronauts more autonomy and confidence in managing their own health when communication with Earth is delayed or limited. This improves crew safety and mission resilience for deep-space travel, and the same approach could support remote or isolated settings on Earth.

Tools and technology
Built with Vite and managed with npm, with automated tests (npm test). Data is stored in browser localStorage, and a service worker makes it a PWA that works offline. It is deployed on Vercel. [languages used: e.g. JavaScript/TypeScript, React, and tailwind.css.] No special hardware is required. Data is entered through the check-in, and demo data simulates stress/sleep drift and infection-like patterns.

Creativity

  • Judging each reading against both a personal baseline and safety limits, rather than a single population range
  • Composite and multi-day rules that detect trouble before any one value looks abnormal
  • A “flight surgeon” report that bridges astronaut self-monitoring and ground support
  • A local-first, offline-capable design that suits the real constraints of spaceflight

Factors we considered

  • Communication delay and limited medical support in deep space
  • The full set of spaceflight risks: radiation, isolation, altered gravity, and a closed environment
  • Behavioral health as well as physical health
  • Privacy and offline reliability, which is why no backend or cloud is used
  • Clarity for a busy crew, hence the plain-language guidance and short daily check-in
  • Safety and honesty about limits: this is a prototype, not a medical device, and would need clinical review and validation before real-world use
